Pour plusieurs experts et intervenants c: For many experts and community workers, this case raises questions and concerns.
Le 28 janvier dernier, Mamadi III Fara C: On January 28, Mamadi III Fara Camara was stopped by police officer Sanjay Vig. He received a ticket for using his phone while driving. A few hours later, he was arrested at home and accused of assaulting the officer during a confrontation by seizing his service weapon and firing at him. He faced several charges, including attempted murder of a police officer.
L’ingénieur de formation maintient son i: The engineer by training maintains his innocence. He says he only witnessed the incident before calling 911. After six days in jail, once the authorities had viewed footage from a surveillance camera and analyzed DNA evidence, the young man was released. The police apologized a few days later, while the real perpetrator of the crime is still at large. “He’s relieved, but overwhelmed by everything that’s happened,” says Me Virginie Dufresne-Lemire, Mr. Camara’s lawyer. “There are so many decisions to make, so many things he never asked to deal with. He did nothing to deserve this.” For many experts and community workers, this case raises questions and concerns.
« Je me suis réveillé ce matin avec un g: “I woke up this morning with a bitter taste in my mouth,” says Stéphanie Germain, a member of the Hoodstock collective. In the wake of these events, she went back to the footage of the May 31 demonstration, held after the death of George Floyd, who was killed by police officers in the United States. “It’s only been eight months. What have we learned?” she asks, before pointing out that we are in the middle of Black History Month. “It’s not a question of bad apples. It’s a question of a culture that has to change here and now, because there will be more victims,” she adds. Despite everything, Stéphanie Germain notes that a change is taking place in the communities.
« Ce qui est beau, c’est de voir comment: “What’s beautiful is seeing how people are organizing,” she says. Several initiatives are being put forward to support Mamadi Camara, but also to help future victims should similar incidents happen again. “The problem of racial profiling hasn’t been solved by the institutions, so people are creating things outside the system to survive,” she says. According to Ms. Germain, the opening of many legal clinics in recent years proves it. The youth worker also observes that a number of young people are deciding to study law.
« Ils ont compris qu’ils ne pouvaient pa: “They understood that they couldn’t change the system if they weren’t part of it.” At the Clinique juridique de Saint-Michel, Me Fernando Belton wants to promote access to justice for people in the neighbourhood. He also believes the current climate shows that the collective awakening after George Floyd’s death didn’t last. “There’s still a lot of work to do, as the various cases we hear about in the media show,” he says. He worries that tensions like those that followed the death of Fredy Villanueva could happen again soon in Quebec.
« Certains groupes opprimés en ont ras l: “Some oppressed groups are fed up, and there are police officers who are also on edge because of the way citizens react to them,” he says. The Camara case brings back bad memories for Me Belton. The criminal and penal lawyer tells us he was himself stopped in downtown Montréal because he matched the description of a suspect. “The description was of a Black man,” he recalls. “In the opposite situation, when the description is of a white man, people aren’t stopped in the same way,” he says. For him, as for Ms. Germain, this incident is part of a series of incidents that has gone on for far too long. “I’m trying to find what has changed and I can’t see it.
Il y a eu plusieurs commissions, et je n: “There have been several commissions, and I don’t see that the recommendations of those commissions have been implemented,” laments Stéphanie Germain. At the demonstration in support of Mamadi Camara, Rito Joseph looks at things from a historical perspective. “It’s part of a historical continuity in Quebec. We’re clinging to colonial remnants,” he believes. “An effort has to be made. If people don’t want to make it, we’ll stay stuck in the situation we’re in right now, that is, with voices being silenced.” “Why does the Black community have to bear that pressure?” he asks. “I’m not sure I know the solution. But it’s not a problem we created. It’s not up to us to find a solution.”
Stéphanie Germain, intervenante culturel: Stéphanie Germain, cultural worker and member of the Hoodstock collective. Photo: Pablo Ortiz
Me Fernando Belton n’a pas accès à l’inf: Me Fernando Belton does not have access to the information used to identify Mr. Camara as a suspect before he was cleared. That information determined the charges brought against him. “You have to understand that in Quebec, the power to lay charges or not rests with the Director of Criminal and Penal Prosecutions, which is an independent body,” he explains. Me Belton believes the government body should explain how it came to the conclusion that the wrong person should be detained and should spend six days in jail before being cleared, when the evidence of his innocence was available.
« Une chose qu’on a pu remarquer au cour: “One thing we’ve been able to observe over the past few years is that the presumption of innocence seems to be something that can be thrown in the trash as soon as serious offences are involved,” the lawyer says. Me Belton points out that, without the video that cleared him, Mr. Camara could have been held in custody for the rest of the legal proceedings, which can last years, or could have been found guilty even though he is innocent. When a person is charged, a bail hearing determines whether they remain in detention. Often, this hearing can be held the day after the arrest. It can also take longer if the charge is serious.
C’est à cette étape que se trouvait M. C: That was the stage Mr. Camara was at when the proceedings were stayed. Disclosure of the evidence also takes place at that point. It is this evidence, available from the start, that cleared Mamadi Camara. An inquiry by the Quebec Superior Court will shed light on the case. <l1>Mamadi Camara says he is disappointed by this.</l1> His lawyer, Me Virginie Dufresne-Lemire, objects to the fact that the inquiry will not be public. “I’m afraid we won’t get any more information from the conclusions of a report.” She is currently reviewing the evidence.
L’avocate défend plusieurs victimes d’ab: The lawyer defends several victims of police abuse and racial profiling. “These are often trivial cases that go completely off the rails, with victims who are racialized people.” She says she is disappointed with the current justice system. “We don’t have a system that helps people who are victims of abuse of authority,” says Me Dufresne-Lemire. “It’s David against Goliath,” she sums up.
Les victimes et les familles de victimes: Victims and their families often have to pay substantial sums for legal recourse, sums they often don’t have and never asked to have to pay. On the other side, members of the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) have the support of the Fraternité des policiers et policières de Montréal. The City of Montréal contributes financially to its resources. Me Dufresne-Lemire represented the family members of Pierre Coriolan at the public inquest into the death of the 58-year-old man, who was shot dead by police officers in 2017. She had to pressure the government to have their legal fees paid.
« La Ligue des droits a fait des demande: “La Ligue des droits made access-to-information requests, and the four lawyers who represented the police officers were paid nearly $200,000. I received $10,000 from the government for the first two weeks,” she says. In many cases, however, victims have to defend themselves relying solely on their own means, which are generally not very substantial. Legal aid is not available in the case of a lawsuit, the lawyer explains, adding that she sometimes has to drop lawsuits because the families she serves lack the means. Several lawyers are currently mobilizing around this issue. Meanwhile, in Montréal’s Black community, people are organizing to raise funds for victims of police abuse. A fundraising campaign aiming to raise $25,000 was launched by lawyer Farrah Auguste to support Mr. Camara. Me Dufresne-Lemire believes we need to look at creating public assistance for this type of case.
« Juripop offre des consultations gratui: “Juripop offers free consultations, funded by the government. We should have this kind of service for cases of police brutality and cases of institutional abuse of authority,” she says.
D’après une étude de 2019 consacrée aux: According to a 2019 study on police stops, Black people are stopped by the SPVM 4.24 times more often than white people. And that figure rises to 15 in some neighbourhoods. While many believe there was racial profiling in the stop of Mamadi Camara, the legal experts La Converse spoke with cannot say, as they don’t have enough information about the incident.
Le criminologue Massimiliano Mulone, qui: Criminologist Massimiliano Mulone, who contributed to the study on racial profiling, believes that in Mr. Camara’s case, the question is this: How do errors come about during a police investigation? “Why are charges laid too quickly? This is what’s often called ‘tunnel vision,’ when investigators are convinced they’ve found the truth,” the specialist explains. This vision takes shape when we look at the elements that confirm our suspicions and dismiss those that refute them.
« Le travail de l’enquêteur, c’est de pr: “The investigator’s job is to prove that a person is guilty. The search for the truth stops quickly when you think you’ve reached the truth,” he suggests. Mr. Mulone’s team was commissioned by the SPVM to carry out a second study on police stops. No study on investigations is planned at the moment. As for analyzing the organization’s culture and its sensitivity to the issue of systemic racism, sociologist Frédéric Boisrond is working on it as an independent strategic adviser. He recently submitted a first report to the SPVM director. “Some say the incident can’t be racist because the officer is of Indo-Pakistani origin. Systemic racism is not individual racism,” he reminds us. “That doesn’t prevent a person, regardless of their ethnic origin, from behaving in a racist way toward a Black person.
Il ne s’agit pas de l’individu, mais de: “It’s not about the individual, but about the culture of the organization they work for. If racist behaviours are tolerated or valued within the organization, or if people are encouraged to behave that way, those behaviours are likely to surface during an interaction,” he says.
Et, au-delà de l’erreur judiciaire, plus: And beyond the miscarriage of justice, many people are denouncing the media coverage of Mamadi Camara’s arrest. “It’s the first time I’ve seen police sources disclose so much information to the media,” continues Me Dufresne-Lemire. “His photo and identity were spread all over the media. They will always be associated with the story of a police officer being attacked,” said Van Harry, a citizen we met at last Sunday’s demonstration in support of Mamadi Camara. “When a person from a marginalized community is accused, their life is laid out for everyone to see. The police, meanwhile, are protected; we get very little information when they’re involved,” adds Stéphanie Germain. She laments that Mr. Camara was portrayed as a criminal before anything more was known about him.
« Nous n’avons pas droit à la présomptio: “We don’t get the presumption of innocence. He was immediately presumed guilty,” she says, hoping Quebec media can learn a lesson from this story. In the United States, meanwhile, a reflection on the coverage of crime and local news is emerging in the journalism community. Kelly McBride has a lot to say on the subject, having worked for 15 years as a reporter assigned to police stories. She believes reporting practices must change. “We do a disservice to our audience by publishing too many crime stories; we harm individuals by making their lives much more difficult,” she said during a course on media coverage of crime that we attended. The Poynter Institute instructor criticizes sensationalist pieces, which are favoured over reporting on public safety or stories that hold institutions to account.
L’ancienne reporter croit que, lorsque d: The former reporter believes that when news is published based on a press release, journalists often amplify the biases the police already have, and that these biases harm the community. According to Ms. McBride, publications should also adopt a content takedown policy. Journalists must also pay attention to their own biases, to the photos published to show the people involved, and to the terms used to describe them.
